theory.overview: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) revolutionized computer vision by exploiting spatial structure in images. Unlike MLPs that treat each pixel independently, CNNs use convolution—sliding filters across the image to detect local patterns like edges, textures, and shapes. These local features are hierarchically combined: early layers find edges, middle layers detect shapes, and deep layers recognize objects. This design drastically reduces parameters (shared weights) and captures translational invariance (a cat is a cat anywhere in the image). CNNs now power everything from medical imaging to self-driving cars.

sections.title: Why Regular Neural Networks Fail for Images
sections.content: A 1000×1000 color image has 3 million pixels. An MLP with one hidden layer of 1000 neurons would need 3 billion parameters—impossible to train! Plus, MLPs don't exploit spatial locality: nearby pixels form meaningful patterns. And they don't have translational invariance: learning 'cat' in the top-left doesn't help recognize 'cat' in the bottom-right.

problems.mlps: Must re-learn patterns at each location

sections.title: Convolution Operation
sections.content: Convolution slides a small filter (kernel) across the image, computing dot products at each position. This detects local patterns like vertical edges, horizontal lines, or color blobs. The same filter is reused across the entire image—parameter sharing!
sections.formula: $(I * K)(i, j) = \sum_{m}\sum_{n} I(i+m, j+n) \cdot K(m, n)$
sections.intuition: At each position, multiply overlapping pixels by filter weights, sum them up
sections.parameters: A 3×3 filter has only 9 weights, applied to every 3×3 patch in the image

sections.title: Convolution Dimensions and Stride
sections.content: Key hyperparameters control the output size and computational cost.

concepts.name: Kernel Size (K)
concepts.effect: Larger kernels = more context but more parameters

concepts.name: Stride (S)
concepts.effect: Stride 2 reduces spatial dimensions by half (downsampling)

concepts.name: Padding (P)
concepts.effect: Preserves spatial dimensions: output size = $(W - K + 2P)/S + 1$

concepts.name: Channels (C)
concepts.effect: Each filter produces one output channel; multiple filters = multiple channels

sections.title: Pooling: Downsampling
sections.content: Pooling reduces spatial dimensions, making the network more computationally efficient and providing some translation invariance. Max pooling (taking the maximum value in each patch) is most common—it preserves the strongest activation.

types.name: Max Pooling
types.operation: Take maximum value in each window
types.effect: Preserves strongest feature detection, provides invariance

types.name: Average Pooling
types.effect: Smoother, preserves more information but less selective

types.name: Global Average Pooling
types.operation: Average entire feature map to one value
types.effect: Reduces each channel to single number—common before classification

sections.typicalSize: 2x2 with stride 2 - halves both height and width

sections.title: CNN Architecture Patterns
sections.content: Modern CNNs follow proven architectural patterns that balance depth, width, and computational efficiency.

patterns.usage: Basic building block, repeats in early layers
As we go deeper: more feature types, fewer spatial locations
Bottleneck layers, reduce/increase channels without spatial change

sections.title: Modern CNN Architectures
sections.content: Landmark architectures pushed the state-of-the-art and introduced key innovations.

architectures.name: LeNet-5 (1998)
architectures.legacy: Established conv → pool → conv → pool pattern

architectures.name: VGGNet (2014)
architectures.legacy: Showed depth matters, simple uniform design

architectures.name: EfficientNet (2019)
architectures.innovation: Compound scaling of depth, width, resolution

keyConcepts.name: Feature Maps
keyConcepts.description: The output of a convolutional layer—each channel represents detection of a specific pattern.
keyConcepts.visualization: Early: edges, corners | Middle: textures, shapes | Deep: object parts

keyConcepts.name: Parameter Sharing
keyConcepts.description: The same filter weights are applied across all spatial locations.
keyConcepts.benefit: Dramatically reduces parameters, provides translation invariance

keyConcepts.name: Receptive Field
keyConcepts.description: The region of the input image that affects a particular feature.
keyConcepts.growth: Grows with depth: deeper neurons 'see' larger image regions

complexity.convolution: $O(H \cdot W \cdot C_{in} \cdot C_{out} \cdot K^2)$—output size × input channels × output channels × kernel size
complexity.memory: $O(H \cdot W \cdot C \cdot L)$ for storing all feature maps during training

steps.title: Input Image
steps.description: Start with RGB image: 3 channels, each with height and width.

steps.title: Apply Convolution Filter
steps.description: Slide 3×3 filter across image, computing dot products.

steps.title: Multiple Filters
steps.description: Each filter produces one output channel. Multiple filters = multiple channels.
steps.latex: \text{Output} \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{out} \times H \times W}$ where $C_{out}$ = number of filters

steps.title: Max Pooling
steps.description: Downsample by taking maximum in each 2×2 window.

steps.title: Stack Layers
steps.description: Repeat conv → relu → pool pattern, increasing channels, decreasing spatial size.

steps.title: Global Average Pooling
steps.description: Reduce each feature map to single value, preparing for classification.

steps.title: Classification
steps.description: Fully connected layer maps features to class scores, then softmax.

practiceProblems.title: Output Size Calculation
practiceProblems.description: Input: 32×32, kernel: 3×3, stride: 1, padding: 1. What is output size?
practiceProblems.explanation: Formula: $\lfloor (W - K + 2P)/S \rfloor + 1$. With padding=1 for 3×3 kernel, output=input size.

practiceProblems.title: Parameter Count
practiceProblems.description: Conv layer: input channels=64, output channels=128, kernel=3×3. How many parameters?
practiceProblems.explanation: Weights: $K^2 \times C_{in} \times C_{out} = 9 \times 64 \times 128 = 73,728$. Biases: one per output channel = 128. Total: 73,856. Note: I had a math error above, correct is 73,728 + 128 = 73,856.
hints: Compare to FC: 64×32×32 → 128×32×32 would be ~8M parameters!

practiceProblems.title: Receptive Field Growth
practiceProblems.description: Three conv layers, all 3×3 with stride 1. What is the receptive field of a neuron in the last layer?
practiceProblems.explanation: Each 3×3 conv adds 1 pixel to radius (or 2 to diameter). Layer 1: RF=3×3. Layer 2: RF=5×5. Layer 3: RF=7×7. With pooling, RF grows faster. This is why deep networks 'see' the whole image.
hints: Each layer's RF = previous RF + kernel_size - 1

practiceProblems.title: 1×1 Convolution
practiceProblems.description: What does a 1×1 convolution with 32 input channels and 64 output channels do? How many parameters?
practiceProblems.answer: It performs a channel-wise linear transformation (like a fully-connected layer per spatial location). Parameters: $1 \times 1 \times 32 \times 64 + 64 = 2,112$.
practiceProblems.explanation: 1×1 conv doesn't combine spatial information—it combines channels. Used for: dimensionality reduction (bottleneck), adding non-linearity, or cross-channel communication. Much cheaper than 3×3 conv.
hints: Like FC layer at each spatial location
Cheap way to change channel count

practiceProblems.title: Architecture Design
practiceProblems.description: Design a CNN for 224×224 images with ~1M parameters that outputs 1000 classes. Specify layer types, sizes, and channel progression.
practiceProblems.answer: Conv1: 64@112×112 → Conv2: 128@56×56 → Conv3: 256@28×28 → Conv4: 512@14×14 → GAP → FC: 512→1000. All 3×3 conv, stride 2 for downsampling.
practiceProblems.explanation: Progressive channel increase (64→128→256→512) compensates for spatial reduction. Stride 2 convs downsample instead of pooling. GAP before FC reduces parameters. Total: ~900K conv params + 512K FC params = ~1.4M.
hints: Double channels when halving spatial size
GAP before final FC saves parameters

practiceProblems.title: Transpose Convolution
practiceProblems.description: What is transposed convolution (deconvolution) and when is it used?
practiceProblems.answer: Transpose convolution upsamples by learning to reverse the convolution operation. Used in: autoencoders (decoding), semantic segmentation (upsampling features to pixel predictions), GANs (generating images).
practiceProblems.explanation: Unlike upsampling+conv, transpose conv learns the upsampling. It effectively 'spreads' each input value over a kernel-sized region. Can produce checkerboard artifacts if stride doesn't divide kernel size evenly.

minigame.title: Feature Detective
minigame.description: Explore how CNNs detect features in images. Design filters, watch feature maps activate, and understand how simple patterns combine into complex recognition.
instructions: Design custom convolution filters (or use presets: edge, blur, sharpen)
Watch the feature map respond to different patterns
Stack multiple conv layers to see hierarchical feature learning
Visualize how the network 'sees' at different depths

codeExample.code:
import numpy as np

class Conv2D:
    """
    2D Convolution layer implementation
    """
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=0):
        self.in_channels = in_channels
        self.out_channels = out_channels
        self.kernel_size = kernel_size
        self.stride = stride
        self.padding = padding
        
        # Xavier initialization
        limit = np.sqrt(6.0 / (in_channels + out_channels) / kernel_size / kernel_size)
        self.weights = np.random.uniform(-limit, limit, 
                                        (out_channels, in_channels, kernel_size, kernel_size))
        self.biases = np.zeros(out_channels)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        """
        Forward pass of 2D convolution
        x: input of shape (batch, in_channels, height, width)
        Returns: output of shape (batch, out_channels, out_h, out_w)
        """
        batch_size, _, h, w = x.shape
        
        # Pad input
        if self.padding > 0:
            x = np.pad(x, ((0,0), (0,0), (self.padding,self.padding), (self.padding,self.padding)), 
                      mode='constant')
        
        # Output dimensions
        out_h = (h + 2*self.padding - self.kernel_size) // self.stride + 1
        out_w = (w + 2*self.padding - self.kernel_size) // self.stride + 1
        
        # Im2col for efficient convolution
        x_col = self._im2col(x)
        w_col = self.weights.reshape(self.out_channels, -1)
        
        # Convolution as matrix multiplication
        out = w_col @ x_col + self.biases.reshape(-1, 1)
        out = out.reshape(self.out_channels, out_h, out_w, batch_size)
        out = out.transpose(3, 0, 1, 2)  # (batch, out_c, out_h, out_w)
        
        return out
    
    def _im2col(self, x):
        """Convert image to column format for efficient convolution"""
        batch_size, channels, h, w = x.shape
        out_h = (h - self.kernel_size) // self.stride + 1
        out_w = (w - self.kernel_size) // self.stride + 1
        
        col = np.zeros((channels * self.kernel_size * self.kernel_size, 
                       batch_size * out_h * out_w))
        
        col_idx = 0
        for i in range(0, h - self.kernel_size + 1, self.stride):
            for j in range(0, w - self.kernel_size + 1, self.stride):
                patch = x[:, :, i:i+self.kernel_size, j:j+self.kernel_size]
                col[:, col_idx:col_idx+batch_size] = patch.reshape(channels * self.kernel_size * self.kernel_size, batch_size)
                col_idx += batch_size
        
        return col

class MaxPool2D:
    """Max pooling layer"""
    def __init__(self, pool_size=2, stride=2):
        self.pool_size = pool_size
        self.stride = stride
    
    def forward(self, x):
        batch, channels, h, w = x.shape
        out_h = (h - self.pool_size) // self.stride + 1
        out_w = (w - self.pool_size) // self.stride + 1
        
        output = np.zeros((batch, channels, out_h, out_w))
        
        for i in range(out_h):
            for j in range(out_w):
                h_start = i * self.stride
                h_end = h_start + self.pool_size
                w_start = j * self.stride
                w_end = w_start + self.pool_size
                
                output[:, :, i, j] = np.max(x[:, :, h_start:h_end, w_start:w_end], axis=(2, 3))
        
        return output

class ReLU:
    def forward(self, x):
        return np.maximum(0, x)

class SimpleCNN:
    """Simple CNN for demonstration"""
    def __init__(self):
        # Architecture: Conv(3->16) -> ReLU -> Pool -> Conv(16->32) -> ReLU -> Pool -> GAP -> FC
        self.conv1 = Conv2D(3, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.relu1 = ReLU()
        self.pool1 = MaxPool2D(pool_size=2, stride=2)
        
        self.conv2 = Conv2D(16, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.relu2 = ReLU()
        self.pool2 = MaxPool2D(pool_size=2, stride=2)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        # Conv block 1
        x = self.conv1.forward(x)
        x = self.relu1.forward(x)
        x = self.pool1.forward(x)
        
        # Conv block 2
        x = self.conv2.forward(x)
        x = self.relu2.forward(x)
        x = self.pool2.forward(x)
        
        # Global Average Pooling
        x = np.mean(x, axis=(2, 3))  # (batch, channels)
        
        return x

# Example: Create a simple edge detection filter
def create_edge_filters():
    """Create horizontal and vertical edge detection filters"""
    horizontal = np.array([[-1, -1, -1],
                          [ 0,  0,  0],
                          [ 1,  1,  1]])
    
    vertical = np.array([[-1,  0,  1],
                        [-1,  0,  1],
                        [-1,  0,  1]])
    
    sobel_x = np.array([[-1, 0, 1],
                       [-2, 0, 2],
                       [-1, 0, 1]])
    
    sobel_y = np.array([[-1, -2, -1],
                       [ 0,  0,  0],
                       [ 1,  2,  1]])
    
    return {
        'horizontal': horizontal,
        'vertical': vertical,
        'sobel_x': sobel_x,
        'sobel_y': sobel_y
    }

# Demonstration
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== Simple CNN Demo ===")
    
    # Create random input image (batch=1, 3 channels, 32x32)
    x = np.random.randn(1, 3, 32, 32)
    
    cnn = SimpleCNN()
    
    print(f"Input shape: {x.shape}")
    
    # Forward pass
    output = cnn.forward(x)
    print(f"Output shape after GAP: {output.shape}")
    
    # Calculate parameters
    conv1_params = np.prod(cnn.conv1.weights.shape) + cnn.conv1.biases.size
    conv2_params = np.prod(cnn.conv2.weights.shape) + cnn.conv2.biases.size
    total_params = conv1_params + conv2_params
    
    print(f"\nParameters:")
    print(f"  Conv1: {conv1_params:,}")
    print(f"  Conv2: {conv2_params:,}")
    print(f"  Total: {total_params:,}")
    
    # Compare to equivalent MLP
    # Input: 32x32x3 = 3072
    # After pooling twice: 8x8x32 = 2048
    # MLP from 3072 to output would need millions of parameters
    print(f"\nCompare to MLP: 3072 inputs would need ~3M parameters just for first layer!")
    print(f"CNN efficiency: {total_params:,} vs ~3,000,000 = {3000000/total_params:.1f}x reduction")
    
    print("\n=== Edge Detection Filters ===")
    filters = create_edge_filters()
    for name, filt in filters.items():
        print(f"\n{name}:")
        print(filt)
